title: Preserve and store food
short: Canning, drying, freezing, pickling and fermenting safely
intro: A beginner's path through tested home food preservation, mostly from the USDA and the National Center for Home Food Preservation. It explains why botulism and acidity decide which method is safe, before moving on to canners, drying, freezing, pickling and fermenting.

limits.text: Pressure canning is the only recommended method for meat, poultry, seafood and vegetables; using boiling-water canners for them risks botulism.
Even a taste of food containing botulinum toxin can be fatal.
CDC recommends discarding any home-canned food that might contain botulism toxin.
Suspect low-acid jars should be treated as containing botulinum toxin; contact with the toxin, even through skin, can be fatal.
Do not change vinegar, food or water proportions in pickle recipes, or use vinegar of unknown acidity; use only tested recipes.
Open-kettle canning and processing jars in ovens, microwaves or dishwashers are not recommended.
Vegetables (except vine-dried beans) and meats are not recommended for drying outdoors; dry them indoors with controlled heat.
Outdated pressure canners should not be used, and dial gauges should be calibrated, for example if dropped or submerged.
